summary: This informational memo describes a two-rate, three-color marker used in data services such as Frame Relay and suited to IP and L2 VPN services. It differs from earlier markers in how it handles in-profile traffic.

eli5.summary: Traffic can be painted green, yellow or red depending on how much a customer sends. This describes a way of choosing the colours.

questions: how does a two rate three color marker work
how do token buckets meter traffic
subtitle: A two-rate, three-color traffic marker that sorts data packets by how much bandwidth they use.

tldr.problem: Internet providers and services need a way to measure and mark data traffic so they can offer different service levels to different classes of packets without overcomplicating the edge device rules.
tldr.mechanism: The marker uses two token buckets with separate rates and sizes to check each packet against a committed rate and an excess rate, marking it green, yellow, or red depending on whether it fits within the allowed bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can sort traffic into three classes for differentiated service with simpler rules at customer edge devices than earlier markers required.

today: RFC 4115 is an Informational RFC. It is not an Internet Standard and carries an IESG note that readers should exercise caution in evaluating it for implementation and deployment. It remains a reference for practical traffic metering in differentiated services networks.

sections.title: What the Marker Does
sections.content:
The trTCM (two-rate, three-color marker) is an algorithm for metering and marking data packets in a computer network. It has been widely used in Frame Relay services and is now used in differentiated services (DiffServ) for IP and L2 VPN services. The marker measures each arriving packet against two rate limits and assigns it a color: green for packets within the committed rate, yellow for packets within an excess rate, and red for packets exceeding both rates.

The marker is different from earlier markers like RFC 2697 (single-rate, three-color) and RFC 2698 (two-rate, three-color). The trTCM improves on RFC 2698 by handling in-profile traffic more efficiently and not requiring customer edge devices to shape traffic to a peak rate.
sections.eli5: A network device watches how fast data flows and stamps each packet with a color: green if it is within the customer's committed rate, yellow if it is within a higher excess rate, and red if it exceeds both.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
The marker is configured with four main parameters. The committed information rate (CIR) is the baseline rate at which tokens are added to a bucket. The committed burst size (CBS) is the maximum tokens that bucket can hold. The excess information rate (EIR) is a second, usually higher, rate at which a second bucket receives tokens. The excess burst size (EBS) is the maximum for that bucket.

CIR and EIR are measured in bits per second and can be set independently, or they can be linked by a burst duration parameter T, where T = CBS/CIR = EBS/EIR. CBS and EBS are measured in bytes and must be larger than the largest packet the marker will see.
sections.eli5: You set a committed speed and burst amount for normal traffic, and a separate excess speed and burst amount for extra traffic.

sections.title: How the Algorithm Works
sections.content:
The marker maintains two token buckets, C and E, that start full. Tokens flow in at rates CIR and EIR respectively, up to sizes CBS and EBS. When a packet arrives, the algorithm checks it in order.

In color-blind mode, all packets start as green. If the packet fits in bucket C, it is marked green and tokens are removed from C. If not, but it fits in bucket E, it is marked yellow and tokens are removed from E. If it fits neither, it is marked red. In color-aware mode, incoming packets that are already colored yellow or red are handled differently—a yellow packet only checks bucket E, and red packets skip all checks.

The key difference from RFC 2698 is that packets within the CIR are marked green immediately, without needing to pass a second test. This means in-profile traffic (traffic within the committed rate) is never dropped just to check a peak rate, making the marker simpler and fairer.
sections.eli5: Two buckets of tokens fill up at different rates. Each packet dips into one bucket or the other. If both buckets are empty, the packet is marked red and might be dropped.

sections.title: Color Meanings and Use
sections.content:
The three colors represent service priorities. Green packets are within the committed rate and should be forwarded with minimal loss. Yellow packets are between the committed and excess rates and might be forwarded as best effort or with higher drop probability. Red packets exceed both rates and may be discarded. Different services can use the colors differently: a premium service might discard all red and some yellow, while a best-effort service might discard only red.

The marker can be used in two modes. In color-blind mode, the algorithm assumes all arriving packets are green. In color-aware mode, the algorithm recognizes packets that already have a color from an earlier marking stage and respects that color when deciding which bucket to check.
sections.eli5: Green packets get through easily, yellow packets might get dropped if the network is busy, and red packets usually get dropped. This lets the network manage congestion fairly.

data.title: Packet processing in color-blind mode
data.code:
Packet of size B arrives
  |
  v
Is B <= Tc(t)?
  |YES -> Mark GREEN, Tc -= B
  |NO
  v
Is B <= Te(t)?
  |YES -> Mark YELLOW, Te -= B
  |NO
  v
Mark RED
